question: In the last legislative term, we adopted a strong stance in favour of decarbonisation and renewable energy, which are both vital when moving towards a sustainable growth model. However, as an outermost region, the Canary Islands face specific structural challenges.

When it comes to the decarbonisation of transport specifically, the islands are hampered by insularity, territorial fragmentation, insufficient charging infrastructure and a high dependence on fossil fuels. This is compounded by the citizens’ reduced financial capacity – the average income was 9.
58 % below the national average in 2023, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute – which makes it difficult to renew an already ageing fleet. In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission intend to look into differentiated application of the EU emissions framework for the outermost regions, in accordance with Article 349 TFEU?
Which funding instruments could be strengthened to support charging infrastructure, energy storage and grid modernisation?
Is it planning any specific financial support measures to facilitate fleet renewal?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) The Commission fully recognises the structural constraints faced by outermost regions such as insularity, territorial fragmentation and dependence on maritime and air links.

The EU Emission Trading System1 (ETS) framework already contains targeted derogations for these situations, including a derogation for maritime and air transport until the end of 2030 for routes within outermost regions and to/from the mainland Member State.

For air transport, airlines flying from airports in outermost regions to the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the United Kingdom benefit from the highest level of ETS support for the uptake of sustainable aviation fuels. Moreover, emissions from flights under public service obligations are also excluded from the ETS.

The 2026 ETS Directive review will assess further connectivity, territorial cohesion and outermost region concerns. As regards road transport, the CO2 standards apply to new vehicles put on the market by manufacturers at the EU level, as such allowing varying regional uptake rates of zero-emission vehicles.

Several financial instruments are available to support investments in zero-emission vehicles and charging infrastructure, including the Recovery and Resilience Fund, ETS national auction revenues, the cohesion policy – notably the European Regional Development Fund, as well as the Social Climate Fund, which addresses households and microenterprises vulnerable to transport poverty, and can for instance support schemes to increase the affordability of zero-emission vehicles for such users.
In addition, the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Facility supports the deployment of charging infrastructure along the main road axis and nodes (Trans-European Transport Network).
